Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for the chase. The Bangladeshi players spread out to the field and take their spots. They will need an inspirational bowling performance to even push the Aussies on the back foot. Beth Mooney and Georgia Voll are the two Australian openers. Marufa Akter will bowl the first over. Voll will take the strike. Off we go again!
... The Run Chase ...

Mid-innings Pitch Report - Mel Jones reporting from pitchside, noting that spin has been quite impressive throughout this T20 World Cup, but here at this venue, it was Australia's seamers who stole the show. She points to the lengths they hit consistently, working that hard short of a length area to great effect. Stresses that the pacers of Bangladesh will also have to operate in a similar way to achieve success on this pitch.

Well-rounded bowling shapes an easy chase - It was a perfectly coordinated, well-rounded effort from the Australian bowling department to dismantle the opposition. Kim Garth, Sophie Molineux, and Ellyse Perry led the wreckage with two wickets apiece, while Annabel Sutherland and Georgia Wareham maintained the chokehold with a wicket each as well. Chasing a tiny target of 78, the Aussies should face no trouble at all and will likely look to wrap things up as quickly as possible to significantly boost their Net Run Rate beyond the reach of their group rivals.

Word from the Australian camp - Kim Garth says it was a really pleasing effort from the bowling attack and describes the way they went about their work as awesome. She adds that restricting Bangladesh to around 80 was a super effort. About the slope, she mentions there has been a little bit of talk about the slope at the ground within the camp, and highlights that they picked up some useful insights from the players who featured at this venue during The Hundred. She notes they were aware there would potentially be something in the wicket early and that the plan was simple, to keep it at the top of the stumps and hit good lengths. Garth ends on a personal note, revealing her parents flew over to watch the game today, and says it is always awesome when they can be there to see her play.

Powerplay collapses and constant stumble - The tone was set early during a disastrous Powerplay, where Bangladesh crawled to just 22 runs in the first 6 overs while losing 3 crucial wickets, immediately putting them on the back foot. Wickets kept tumbling thereafter as the Australian bowlers relentlessly tightened the screws, choking the scoring rates and allowing no breathing room. Backed by an exceptional fielding unit that kept the pressure intact, Australia never let the innings get away, leaving only two Bangladeshi batters in double figures, with the skipper Nigar Sultana, topping the chart with 27, which highlights the batting unit's overall struggle.

Dominant Aussies stifle Bangladesh - The Australian camp will be absolutely delighted with their clinical bowling performance after restricting Bangladesh to a meager 77 for 8 in their 20 overs. The Tigresses' innings simply never found any rhythm or momentum, as they constantly lost wickets at regular intervals. Struggling to cope with the precise line and length of the tournament favorites, the Bangladesh batters found it incredibly difficult to rotate the strike or find the boundaries regularly.

Play and a miss! A dot to end the innings. Bangladesh Women finish at 77/8 on the board. Full around off stump. She sets off for a cheeky run anyway but is sent back. Mooney has a shy at the stumps at the batting end, but cannot find the target.

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK. Nothing much has changed for Bangladesh. But Nigar Sultana and Ritu Moni have ensured to somewhat stop the slide. Still, they are nowhere in a position to throw a challenge to the Aussies as boundaries are hard to come by and runs are dripping in ones and twos rather than flowing. Australia Women have unleashed their best with the ball by using as many as seven bowlers so far and will look to dismiss Nigar as quickly as possible to restrict Bangladesh below triple figures. Commentary.Commentary: Right. Done with all the pre-match rituals. Amar Shonar Bangla and Advance Australia Fair are sung/chanted proudly. It is now time for Match 9 to get underway at Leeds. The two umpires walk out. Sophie Molineux has her ladies in a huddle near the ropes. Now, they spring out confidently to take their respective fielding spots. Juairiya Ferdous and Dilara Akter are the two Bangladeshi openers making way to the crease. Megan Schutt has the new ball and is raring to. No slip in place. Let's place says the umpire. Here we go...

Time for the national anthems - The giant flags of both countries are unveiled in the centre, which is met with big cheers from the faithful of both teams in the crowd. Out walk the match officials and right after them, the two captains lead their respective groups out to get lined up for the anthems. It will be Bangladesh's first, followed by Australia's.

From the Aussie camp, it's Annabel Sutherland - She says it is a beautiful place to play cricket and that it is always great to be back. She adds it is a wonderful venue to watch players go about their business and notes the ground offers something with the ball, particularly with the new ball early on. On the strength of Australia's lineup, Sutherland says the beauty of their side is the options they have throughout the order, with plenty of all-rounders who can contribute with both spin and pace. She highlights just how deep their batting goes, pointing out that Sophie Molineux came in at number 11 in the previous game, which she describes as ridiculous. She credits the top order for doing their job and signs off with a smile, saying she is hoping to get a hit herself today.

Let's hear it from Sharmin Akhter of Bangladesh - On their last win against Netherlands, Sharmin says she feels Bangladesh were the better side and is happy to have contributed to the result. On facing Australia today, she says it is a good opportunity for the team, adding that they came here to show the world what Bangladesh cricket is about and that playing against the best teams is an exciting prospect. On adapting to the conditions, she keeps it light, saying it is good to finally see the sun and that the team are feeling better for it.

PITCH REPORT - Ian Bishop is pitchside with Julia Price to inspect the conditions out there. On the dimensions, Ian notes the square boundaries are relatively short, measuring 62 metres on one side and 59 meters on the other, with the breeze coming across from that shorter side. Julia Price draws attention to the sheer scale of the playing block, describing it as enormous, with 14 match pitches across the ground alongside multiple practice wickets and run-through pitches. She adds that while it is a very large playing area, the square boundaries remain quite short. On the outfield, Price notes there has been a little overnight rain, which may make things fractionally slow early on, but once the ball gets through the infield, it should race away to the boundary. Bishop then turns to the pitch itself, describing it as a beautiful surface cut down to around seven millimetres, as is usual for a T20 game. He says there is plenty of grass coverage to help keep the ball intact and reckons fast bowlers are going to love it, with true pace and good bounce on offer. He adds that the average at this ground sits at around 24.7 runs per wicket, making it the best venue in the tournament for fast bowlers so far. On expected scoring, Bishop says that even with some early assistance for the bowlers due to the overnight rain, he is thinking this is a 180 to 200-run pitch, predicting a nice balance between bat and ball.

Australia Women (Playing XI) - Beth Mooney (WK), Georgia Voll, Ellyse Perry, Grace Harris (In for Phoebe Litchfield), Georgia Wareham, Annabel Sutherland, Nicola Carey, Sophie Molineux (C), Alana King, Kim Garth and Megan Schutt (In for Ashleigh Gardner).

Bangladesh Women (Playing XI) - Dilara Akter, Juairiya Ferdous, Sharmin Akhter, Nigar Sultana (C/WK), Sobhana Mostary, Shorna Akter, Ritu Moni, Nahida Akter (In for Sanjida Akter Meghla), Rabeya Khan, Sultana Khatun (In for Fariha Trisna) and Marufa Akter.

The captain of Bangladesh Women - Nigar Sultana says that they would have loved to bat first. On the mindset, she is clear. Stresses on executing the plans, backing the batting unit, and the belief is firmly there that Bangladesh have every chance in this one. On facing Australia despite a difficult record against them, she says every team gets an equal opportunity in a tournament like this, and what matters is how they actually go about this game. Adds that the mindset is positive, the belief is there, and if they can pull together and execute their plans, she feels they have a genuine chance. On the batting unit's increased intent, she points to a long period of debate and consultation around the top order before they found their answer in Ferdous, someone who can genuinely take the attack on and has been doing exactly that. One change to the XI, she informs that they have a couple of changes.

The captain of Australia Women - Sophie Molineux says they will be bowling first as the track looks a bit softer and they'll be looking to make the most of the conditions. She adds that it is a beautiful ground and the outfield looks fast too, so they'll need to be alert out in the field. About the team combination, Sophie informs that Phoebe Litchfield is injured, so she misses out, but she'll be fine for the India game and Ashleigh Gardner had a fall, and because of a sore ankle, she is not featuring as well. Sophie Molineux also adds that Grace Harris and Megan Schutt replace Ashleigh Gardner and Phoebe Litchfield.

TOSS - Both captains, Sophie Molineux and Nigar Sultana, are out for the coin flip. Ian Bishop leads the proceedings. Molineux spins the coin, but Sultana calls it incorrectly. Australia Women have opted to BOWL first.

Back to Headingley - It's a beautiful morning in Leeds, with the sun shining brightly and the crowd gradually building up at the venue. A few clouds dotted around but nothing to worry about. Good cricket weather, all day long.

Bangladesh are 4 down at halfway - Wait... what? Four down already? Easy, easy. This match at Leeds has not even started yet, as the toss is still to come in a few minutes. That one is coming in from Chattogram, where the Bangladesh and Australia men are simultaneously going at it in the first T20I of the three-match series. Bangladesh are batting first and as per the latest reports, they are 75/4 after 10 overs in the first innings. It is just one of those delightful coincidences where both the men and women are taking on the same opposition on the same day. And make no mistake, the one happening right here carries considerably more weight in the current context. So by the time we wait for the coin flip here, you can simply switch tabs to follow the updates from the men's game. Or if you're an ODI geek, do follow the updates from the 2nd ODI between India vs Afghanistan as well, but make sure you join us back at the toss in time.

A classic David vs Goliath showdown - While Australia start as overwhelming favourites, the unpredictable nature of the format means Bangladesh possess the tools to cause serious frustration if they execute perfectly. But it will take a flawless performance from the Tigresses to shatter the odds and beat the Aussies in T20Is for the first time ever. And with both teams playing their first-ever T20I at Headingley, all the ingredients are in place for a gripping contest. Toss and team news to follow.

Bangladesh's gritty resolution - Four tournaments. Zero wins. That was Bangladesh's reality across 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2023, yet the Tigresses have gradually carved out a reputation as a high-mettle side that simply refuses to buckle regardless of who the opposition is. But, having beaten just one Full Member opposition in T20 World Cup history, Sri Lanka back in 2014, the odds remain firmly stacked against them. However, they arrive here having just executed their highest successful chase in T20 World Cup cricket, and there is genuine spring in their step. Much like a certain set of Kangaroos, wink wink. All eyes will fall on skipper Nigar Sultana, Bangladesh's most prolific run-scorer against Australia in T20 internationals, with a couple of half-centuries already against them, one of which came in the 2023 edition. If Bangladesh are to pull off something special here, their captain will almost certainly be at the heart of it.

The imperious Australian juggernaut - Australia remain the undisputed benchmark of international cricket, having dominated global tournaments for years with an unmatched winning culture. The numbers back the reputation, too. Just one defeat in their last seventeen T20 World Cup matches, a streak stretching all the way back to November 2018. Even in this tournament, they comfortably wear the crown of the team to beat, boasting an incredibly deep batting lineup where world-class match-winners walk out even at number eight or nine. However, to truly transform into an untouchable side, the Aussies will be hyper-focused on finding immediate stability at the top of the order to prevent early hiccups against the new ball.

Heavyweights clash with rising challengers - Hello and welcome, everyone. The stage is set for another triple-header day in the ICC Women's T20 World Cup, 2026. It all starts with two teams coming off highly successful campaign openers. Australia Women head into this fixture with a positive momentum, looking to firmly establish their dominance at the top of the table after a clinical victory over South Africa in their tournament opener. Similarly, Bangladesh Women enter the contest riding a wave of high confidence, aiming to carry the rhythm from their opening victory against the Netherlands straight into this massive challenge.
... MATCH DAY ...

Battle of the unbeatens - The ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 has already set the tournament alight in England with standard-setting displays and a highly competitive race in Group A. Match 9 brings together two teams that have successfully negotiated their initial hurdles and are looking to stamp their authority on the pool stage firmly. Australia Women arrive at Headingley fresh off a clinical 65-run demolition of South Africa, anchored by Georgia Wareham's lethal 3 for 13 spell. Meanwhile, Bangladesh Women are riding high on confidence after kickstarting their campaign with a comprehensive six-wicket triumph over the Netherlands, leaving both teams eager to stretch their winning streaks. Australia’s untouchable setup - Australia Women remain the benchmark of global cricket, possessing a squad combination so perfectly balanced that they can choke teams out from any situation. Under captain Sophie Molineux, their lineup is littered with elite multi-dimensional operators like Ellyse Perry, Ashleigh Gardner, and Phoebe Litchfield, giving them a safety net that few teams in the world can replicate. This ability to have a new match-winner emerge in every game means they are rarely flustered when top-order wickets tumble. If there is any area where the powerhouse could look to optimize, it is ensuring their opening combination converts starts into massive Powerplay scores to put matches entirely out of reach before the spin restrictions ease. The spin sensation of Bangladesh - Bangladesh Women have enjoyed a dream start to this tournament, but climbing a mountain as steep as Australia will require an immaculate performance at the peak of their powers. Their greatest path to a historic upset lies within their slow-bowling engine room, powered by the guile of Rabeya Khan and Nahida Akter. For Bangladesh to restrict the deep Australian batting roster, their tweakers must extract grip out of the Headingley surface and squeeze the scoring rates through the middle overs. Alongside their spin mastery. Captain Nigar Sultana must anchor the batting order and absorb pressure to give her explosive lower-order a platform to launch late in the innings. Form (Last 5 completed T20Is, recent first) - AUS-W - WWWLW | BAN-W - LWWLL. Strategic crossroads - The ultimate headline duel features Bangladesh's most competent batter against spin, Nigar Sultana, trying to negotiate the drift and variations of leg-spinner Georgia Wareham, who single-handedly broke the back of South Africa's middle-order in the previous round. Concurrently, look out for the Powerplay clash where teenage pace sensation Marufa Akter will test the resolve of seasoned Australian opener Beth Mooney. If Marufa can extract early movement, it could expose the Australian middle-order to a trial by spin far earlier than they would prefer.
